**What T9 did.** It worked through the top 177 functions on the naming list:
- **Every one has a name or a recorded reason to stay unnamed.** Each named function has a comment saying what it does and why we think so.
- **The new names are marked best guesses.** No outside record names these functions.
- **Nine names are cited from Sony's library** that the game links.
- **Most of the effort went into the tools.** The same placeholder name can mean different functions in different overlays. The rename tool, the leftover-name scanner and the lint now handle each binary separately, which is what made the heavily copied functions nameable.

**Why the scan hung for 11 hours.** The scanner handed git's search tool 96 separate patterns at once. With one pattern, git searches each file in a single fast pass. With several separate patterns, it falls back to a much slower way of matching, line by line. Over the 669 MB of source, that meant the search never finished. The scanner now joins its patterns into one per chunk, so a batch of 48 renames scans in about 7 seconds. It also stops with an error after 30 minutes instead of waiting forever. The fix is noted in the cookbook, the project's notes on techniques and traps, as C0575.

All 102 open functions in the top 177 of the naming list now have a disposition: 80 got best-guess `guess_` names and 22 stay unnamed with a recorded reason. Each named function has the T7-style header comment at every definition. The final checks pass at a2af7fed1c: R22 218/218, `make tools-health` OK, and `rename_scan --ledger --gate-citations` and `--worklist` both OK. Every function row with rank43 <= 177 is disposed.

**Counts.**
- None of the 102 could be cited: no outside record names these functions.
- Guesses by evidence: 66 xref chain, 14 code inference. By confidence: 16 high, 50 medium, 14 low.
- Nine further names are cited from the linked Sony library (R125): SetRotMatrix, SetTransMatrix, GsInitCoordinate2, GsGetLw, GsSetProjection, ApplyMatrixLV, RotMatrixZYX, rsin and rcos.
- Two units marked no-evidence earlier got names on new evidence from batch 3: func_8002D4C8 is now guess_RequestSound (it sends sound requests through SpuSetKey), and D_8011D030 is now guess_g_SmallObjectPool.
- No earlier `guess_` name needed renaming; batches 2 and 4 confirmed two of them.

**Why the scan hung.** The leftover-name scan ran 11 hours on batch 1 with no output. It handed git grep its 96 search patterns as separate arguments, and git grep 2.43 slows by orders of magnitude when given more than one. Given a single pattern, it searches a whole file at once. Given several, it falls back to checking each line against each pattern. On the cheap test, one rename's two patterns took 26 s passed separately, while all 48 renames joined into one pattern took 7 s. The scan now joins its patterns into one per 32 renames and fails with a clear error after 30 minutes instead of hanging. On two earlier batches it gave byte-identical results, and those scans fell from 6 and 11 minutes to 13.5 seconds.

**Tool changes the batches needed** (approach changes inside the done-when, recorded under Deviations):
- **Per-binary renames (R124).** The same placeholder can mean different functions in different overlays. The rename tool, the leftover-name scan and the lint now treat each binary separately, which is what let functions with many copies, like rank 3's 14 addresses, be named.
- **Same-address tokens.** The scan recognises a token that names a different function or datum at the same address only from a fact on its own line. Examples are an object id's path, a member's binary, or a ledger row's hash; there is no exemption list.
- **Census aliases.** The census now reads definitions bound to an assembly label of any name, keeping a renamed label as spelled.
- **Module sigs.** `sig-modules` in the Makefile now takes module function names from the symbol files. Without that, renamed module copies dropped out of the instruction totals and `tools-health` failed.

**Corrections and restarts.** The developer's mid-task corrections were applied: the hung scan was killed by pid with batch 1's edits kept, and the hang was diagnosed and fixed. Two session restarts each cut off a coder: one before any edit, one after its rename was applied but before commit. Each was replaced by a new coder working from the files left behind. In all, 14 in-house coders ran.

Banked in the cookbook: C0575 (the git grep stall) and C0576 (module sigs). C0571 (per-binary renames) and C0572 (asm labels and the progress-numbers drift) gained paragraphs.

T7 pilot naming batch and the conventions, for the developer's review: The pilot batch is in: 27 worklist units disposed, which is a little under the "about 30" the plan asked for. Two are cited, 23 are best guesses and two are marked no-evidence with a reason. Every disposed unit has its names.tsv row. Every named function has a 3-line comment above each of its definitions: what it does, confidence and basis, and its ledger pointer. That is 18 sites in total: the 13 shared class headers, one private copy in ov_SC07_006 and four functions in src/800.c. The verify gate `rename_scan.py --ledger --gate-citations` passes, as do the worklist check, lint_symbol_refs and the batch's rename scan (0 stale, 0 unclassified). R22 is 218/218 on the batch commit, and tools-health passes. **Conventions.** They are written in docs/wiki/Names-and-renames.md under "Naming conventions": - style follows docs/gen3-standards.md; - `guess_` is always the outermost prefix (`guess_g_X`, `guess_s_X`), so removing it gives the confirmed name; - a name is cited only when its meaning comes from a recorded source; any name we word from reading the code is a guess, whatever its confidence; - a basis quotes code facts with their lines, never the name restated; - the header-comment template; - one name covers a class at several addresses only when it describes the shared body; - placeholders are specific to each binary; - the no-evidence disposition. **The names.** - Cited: g_PlayerHp and g_PlayerHpMax, from live-RAM rows in the memory map. - A camera group, the strongest of the guesses because it rests on library calls: guess_UpdateCamera, guess_g_ActiveCamera, guess_g_MainCamera, guess_g_CameraWsMatrix, guess_GetCameraYaw and guess_WorldToScreen. - Rotation and yaw helpers: guess_RotTransSVWithMatrix, guess_RotTransSVWithObjMatrix, guess_YawToPoint, guess_TurnStepToTarget and guess_Vec3sDotAdd. The last is the multi-address case: three addresses, named with `_2` and `_3`. - Object state: guess_SetState and guess_ApplyVelocity. - Main-only functions: guess_TestGameFlag, guess_SetGameFlag, guess_GetStoryProgress, guess_InitModelObject and guess_MoveImageList. - A low-confidence player group: guess_g_PlayerActor and guess_g_PlayerPosX/Y/Z. - guess_g_ClockMinute. - No-evidence: func_80014554, an empty body at 726 unrelated addresses, and func_8002D4C8. **What went wrong.** - **Rank 3 dropped.** The first coder found that the rename tool rewrites an old name in every file. The extra copies of func_80146CA0 share their placeholder names with unrelated functions in other overlays, so renaming them would rename those too. I dropped that unit and left its row open (cookbook C0571). - **md modules.** md_* modules that call the overlay functions got their own symbol-file rows with the same names. - **Type census.** tools-health first failed because the type census recognised globals only by the `D_` spelling. The third coder fixed the census and the restruct ledger, then ran the census before and after the batch. The numbers are identical: 14,376 types, 3,298 unassigned sites, 0 uncovered residue, 9,302 lying (cookbook C0572). - **Changes outside the file list.** The coders also changed tools/ (rename_sym, rename_scan, type_census, lever_census, dedup_integrate) outside the task's file list. Each fix cleared a check the batch procedure requires. Two of them were speed-ups proven to give identical output: a dry run went from 17 minutes to 52 seconds. **Decisions for the developer,** each with my recommendation: - Adopt the conventions page as the rule for T8-T11. I recommend yes. - Keep func_80014554 unnamed. I recommend yes. - Keep g_PlayerHpMax cited. It rests on two live states, the max/current pairing and the code clamp. I recommend yes. - Keep the low-confidence player group rather than reverting it to placeholders. I recommend yes. - Add a rename limited to the binaries a row covers to rename_sym before the function batches, so units like func_80146CA0 can be named. I recommend yes, as T9's first step. - Rename the `func_`/`D_` aliases of linked PsyQ functions as cited library names, after checking that the symbol file can carry a name the object already defines. Examples are func_8004914C (SetRotMatrix) and D_800AE688 (GsWSMATRIX). I recommend yes. - Accept the coders' tool fixes. I recommend yes. **Still open:** - delever's R26 detector still matches only the `D_`/`g_` spellings; nothing counts it today. - A full rename scan of a batch takes about 85 minutes. T9 name the worklist's functions, rank43 1 to 177: All 102 open functions in the top 177 of the naming list now have a disposition: 80 got best-guess `guess_` names and 22 stay unnamed with a recorded reason. Each named function has the T7-style header comment at every definition. The final checks pass at a2af7fed1c: R22 218/218, `make tools-health` OK, and `rename_scan --ledger --gate-citations` and `--worklist` both OK. Every function row with rank43 <= 177 is disposed. **Counts.** - None of the 102 could be cited: no outside record names these functions. - Guesses by evidence: 66 xref chain, 14 code inference. By confidence: 16 high, 50 medium, 14 low. - Nine further names are cited from the linked Sony library (R125): SetRotMatrix, SetTransMatrix, GsInitCoordinate2, GsGetLw, GsSetProjection, ApplyMatrixLV, RotMatrixZYX, rsin and rcos. - Two units marked no-evidence earlier got names on new evidence from batch 3: func_8002D4C8 is now guess_RequestSound (it sends sound requests through SpuSetKey), and D_8011D030 is now guess_g_SmallObjectPool. - No earlier `guess_` name needed renaming; batches 2 and 4 confirmed two of them. **Why the scan hung.** The leftover-name scan ran 11 hours on batch 1 with no output. It handed git grep its 96 search patterns as separate arguments, and git grep 2.43 slows by orders of magnitude when given more than one. Given a single pattern, it searches a whole file at once. Given several, it falls back to checking each line against each pattern. On the cheap test, one rename's two patterns took 26 s passed separately, while all 48 renames joined into one pattern took 7 s. The scan now joins its patterns into one per 32 renames and fails with a clear error after 30 minutes instead of hanging. On two earlier batches it gave byte-identical results, and those scans fell from 6 and 11 minutes to 13.5 seconds. **Tool changes the batches needed** (approach changes inside the done-when, recorded under Deviations): - **Per-binary renames (R124).** The same placeholder can mean different functions in different overlays. The rename tool, the leftover-name scan and the lint now treat each binary separately, which is what let functions with many copies, like rank 3's 14 addresses, be named. - **Same-address tokens.** The scan recognises a token that names a different function or datum at the same address only from a fact on its own line. Examples are an object id's path, a member's binary, or a ledger row's hash; there is no exemption list. - **Census aliases.** The census now reads definitions bound to an assembly label of any name, keeping a renamed label as spelled. - **Module sigs.** `sig-modules` in the Makefile now takes module function names from the symbol files. Without that, renamed module copies dropped out of the instruction totals and `tools-health` failed. **Corrections and restarts.** The developer's mid-task corrections were applied: the hung scan was killed by pid with batch 1's edits kept, and the hang was diagnosed and fixed. Two session restarts each cut off a coder: one before any edit, one after its rename was applied but before commit. Each was replaced by a new coder working from the files left behind. In all, 14 in-house coders ran. Banked in the cookbook: C0575 (the git grep stall) and C0576 (module sigs). C0571 (per-binary renames) and C0572 (asm labels and the progress-numbers drift) gained paragraphs. T12 ledger-to-comment pass: each lever's wall and each guess's ledger pointer beside the code: The source now shows each kept compiler lever's wall and each best-guess name's ledger row beside the code. The game still rebuilds byte-identical: R22 gave 218 of 218. **Walls.** Each `// !FAKE:` marker on a site that a residue row excuses now ends with that row's ` wall:<tag>`. The instrument text is still there, so attribution still finds every marker. That is 1,846 marker lines covering 1,850 sites in 660 files; four lines are each shared by two sites with the same wall, and no line needed two tags. - `tools/lever_census.py --check --strict --residue`, which `make tools-health` already runs, now checks every marker line: its tags must exactly match the tags of the residue rows its sites use. It fails on a missing marker, a marker with no wall, a different wall, or a leftover wall on a site no row excuses, and it prints the expected tag. - The selftest covers the pass, no-wall, wrong-wall and leftover-wall cases. Phase 3.43 is finished and needs your word to close it. Its milestone gate passed in full, every check on its first run, at commit f88462bafc. All 218 game binaries still rebuild byte-identical, and all six Ghidra proofs pass.

**What the phase did.** This is the phase where the code got its first real names.
- **The top 500 are all settled.** The 500 functions and data items that matter most are all decided:
  - **2 cited:** the player's HP and HP cap, proven in live memory.
  - **393 best guesses:** each is marked `guess_` and has a ledger row giving what in the code it rests on and how sure we are.
  - **105 left unnamed on purpose:** each has a written reason, usually that the code alone doesn't show what the item is for.
- **Why so many guesses.** There's no public symbol map for this game, and 448 of the 500 had nothing to go on but their own code. A guess is a proposal, clearly marked, that a later phase or a live-memory session can confirm.
- **Inherited names now have proof.** All 1,083 names from earlier phases now cite their source, and the health check fails on any uncited name. Most are Sony library names, checked against the library's own files. Two that rested only on community hearsay were demoted to guesses.
- **Comments beside the code.** Every named function has a three-line header saying what it does, how sure we are, and where its ledger row is. Every guessed variable points to its row. Every remaining compiler hint now says beside the code why it can't be removed, and a check keeps those notes in step.
- **The two items carried over from 3.41:**
  - **The 38 functions without returns.** 21 now have a real `return`; the other 19 have a comment explaining why a `return` would change the bytes.
  - **The 9 doubtful wall tags.** These are the labels saying why a compiler hint can't be removed. Each was re-checked: 4 kept their label and 5 got a more accurate one.
- **Tools.** Renames now work one binary at a time, because the same placeholder name can mean different functions in different overlays. The 11-hour scan hang was found and fixed: a search that used to take that long now takes seconds. Three scratch scripts were kept as proper tools, including the evidence-gathering one for future naming batches.
- **Ghidra and the record.** Your live Ghidra project has the new names. The story, retrospective, wiki and decision log run to Phase 43.

**Left open:**
- **Unnamed helpers.** A few text helpers are still unnamed. Naming them later would let several of today's unnamed functions get names too.
- **A census count that varies.** The struct census gives slightly different counts on an unchanged tree. That needs a small fix.
- **The live-memory session.** I offered you a short session to confirm data names in live memory. I still owe you its scenario list, and it can now aim at the 393 guesses.

**After the close:**
- I'll start the MCP Ghidra again and ask you to run `/mcp`.
- The 16 GB phase scratch folder `.run/3.43` can be deleted; everything worth keeping is already in the repo. That includes the 994 MB Ghidra backup, and only about 8 GB of disk is free.
- You push this repo, and the archive clone at `/home/musashi/BFM-decomp-archive` (commit 0a63007).

The close question is open in the picker.

Phase 3.43 is closed. I've started the MCP Ghidra again, so please run `/mcp` once it has finished loading, in about a minute.

I've also started the planner for Phase 3.44. It's drafting to `/home/musashi/bfm-decomp/.run/plans/phase-3.44.md`.

**What 3.44 is for.** It answers the concern you raised on 11-10. Matching bytes proves the source builds the same game. It doesn't prove that each function's declaration tells a modder the truth about what it takes and what it gives back. 3.44 proves every function's signature from the machine code, so you can edit against the prototypes with confidence. It comes before the file-layout phase (3.45), so declarations are settled before files move.

**What it builds:**
- **A signature census.** This is a new tool that reads the machine code of all 218 binaries and writes one row per function. Each row records:
  - whether any caller uses the return value;
  - how many arguments the function takes;
  - how wide each one is, and whether it's signed.

  Each answer cites the instructions it rests on. Where the machine code can't decide, such as calls through function pointers, the row says "unknown" and why. It's needed because no tool today reads signatures from the machine code; every one we have compares C text with C text.
- **The fix-up.** Every declaration and definition is made to agree with the census. Where the shipped game itself was inconsistent, there's one shared prototype plus a marked cast at the few call sites that need the old view. Each such exception is ledgered, and the tool checks its cited instructions against the real bytes. That includes the 19 return-type mismatches from 3.41.
- **The 356 functions without a return.** These were parked from 3.43. Each gets settled from the census: a real `return`, a comment saying what the return register holds and why, or `void` where no caller ever reads the result.
- **A permanent check.** The project health check fails on any disagreement that isn't ledgered.

**What it must not change:**
- the game's bytes: all 218 binaries must still rebuild byte-identical, and the Ghidra proofs must still pass;
- names and file locations.

**How big it is.** It's real analysis, not a grep. Reading return-value use correctly means following branches and the MIPS delay slot, the instruction that runs right after a jump. Then the fix-up touches many declarations, but its size comes from the census, so the planner sizes that part once the measurement exists.

When the draft is ready, I'll open it in the plan view and tell you in a line or two what needs your decision. It will most likely include stopping Ghidra once for the proofs, as before.

Still yours: push the repo and the archive clone at `/home/musashi/BFM-decomp-archive` (commit 0a63007). The 16 GB `.run/3.43` scratch folder can be deleted whenever you like; nothing in it is needed.

Milestone: a fleet-wide asm signature census (`tools/sig_evidence.py`, one row per function or share class over all 218 binaries) records whether the return is used (a caller reads `$v0` after the call), the argument count (registers the callee reads, registers callers set, stack slots) and argument and return widths and signs, each with its cited instructions, and `unknown` with a reason where the asm cannot decide (indirect calls, liveness); every declaration and definition agrees with its measured contract or carries a ledgered exception whose cited instructions the tool verifies against the bytes (0 unledgered disagreements, gated in `make tools-health`), `config/lying_exceptions.tsv` causes included; the no-`return` functions parked from 3.43 T3 resolved (a byte-neutral `return` or a `$v0` comment from the census); R22 218/218; ghidra `--proof` PASS

## Rationale
- Order: baselines (T1); type_census's struct_map tie-break (T2) before any census diff, so neutrality checks compare clean (rule R70); the asm census (T3), then the C comparison with the exception ledger and the developer's word on the measured buckets (T4); the fix-ups, smallest known first: the 19 width lies (T5, which also settles the marked-cast spelling), the arity casts (T6, the same macro family), I5 (T7), the rest of T4's buckets (T8); the gate into tools-health once it can be green (T9); milestone gate (T10); close docs (T11); cleanup (T12).
- The review at T4 (`review: yes`): the developer asked for the fix-up to be sized from the measurement (DECIDED), and he picks stop rules once the residue is bucketed (the card). The review shows per bucket the functions, declaration lines and objects to touch, the rung, and which buckets ledger instead of editing; after his word Claude adjusts T5-T8 with plan_edit (inside the milestone).
- A new tool, three lines (house rule §3). What it does: decodes each distinct body once and follows its control flow to measure $v0 reads after calls, the argument registers and stack slots a callee reads, each call site's argument setup, and narrowing around calls. What exists: argcheck and type_census compare C texts (R3.44-002); tools/sig_image.py decodes the original bytes into function boundaries, h_exact hashes and jal targets with rabbitizer (:34-37); tools/decl_from_use.py has a MIPS-I word decoder and a linear register scan for data externs (:130, :188); m2c needs a supplied signature (translate.py:4692) and decompiles whole functions. The delta: a control-flow graph with delay slots and a $v0/$a-register liveness pass over the sig inputs, and the comparison with the C through argcheck's parsers. The milestone names the tool.
- Rows by h_exact (share_census.py:12-13): one byte body has one callee contract; its callers are the union over every instance's binary. A call from an overlay or module into main or resident resolves through the target binary's sig rows.
- The evidence bar: `used` needs a cited read of $v0 on some path after a call before $v0 is written; `unused` needs every call site known (no jalr exposure, the address never taken) and none reading; anything else is `unknown:<reason>`. Width and sign evidence is recorded with cites and decides nothing alone (R3.44-001). The census never reads the C.
- "Agrees with its measured contract" is the rule table T4 writes (docs/ops/sig-evidence.md, a selftest per rule) and the developer sees at T4's review. The planned reading: a definition or declaration disagrees when it contradicts a measured fact (a `void` return that a caller reads; fewer parameters than the callee reads; a declaration that differs from the definition); a `()` declaration is not a prototype, so under "one shared prototype" it is replaced (T6) unless ledgered; an unused parameter or an unread non-void return contradicts nothing. K&R definitions stay where the table finds no contradiction: their heads are byte-true (C0508:1).
- Marked casts: rule R123 lets a kept cast be spelled only by a registered include/common.h macro backed by a ledger row; the registered macros are memory-access forms (include/common.h:69-78), so the call-site view needs one new registered macro, introduced by T5 after a one-callee probe and recognized by type_census's KEPT forms (:143-145). If no cast spelling keeps a direct `jal` (a cast function designator may compile to `jalr`), T5 returns `question` with the alternative (an asm-label alias declaration naming the old view, C0223).
- One exception ledger for the gate: config/lying_exceptions.tsv gains a cites field or moves into the new ledger, with type_census's loader (positional fields 0-2, :2044-2055) kept working in the same commit.
- tools-health: the gate runs after type_census (Makefile:317); target at most 5 min at -j 16 (tools-health is about 19 min).
- Effort: T3 is the one `effort: high` task: what counts as a read, when the census must say `unknown`, and how tail positions and address-taken functions resolve are judgments no test fully arbitrates, and every later task copies them. T4's rule table is judged at its review.

## Risks
- Evidence soundness: a liveness or call-resolution bug can report `unused` and license a wrong `void`. Guards: `unused` needs every call site known; the void rung is byte-checked per object (rule R104); T3's per-rule selftests, controls and 20-row hand check.
- Ambiguity is normal for widths and tail positions (R3.44-001): many rows will be `unknown`, which the milestone allows; the summaries count them by reason.
- Cross-binary resolution: overlays share load addresses (3.43: the location-overlay slot 0x80128158); a jal resolves inside its own binary or into main or resident, anything else is `unknown`.
- Scale: about 3.7 million declaration lines; the fix-ups touch thousands of TUs, and a shared-header touch re-fans 4,555 objects (R3.42-006). Per-object compares come before R22; batch sizes are set at T4's review.
- Marked casts: a cast function designator may compile to `jalr` instead of `jal` (T5's probe decides; the fallback goes to the developer as a question); the number of call sites needing the int view for the 19 (9,302 declaration rows) is unknown until T4.
- Byte movement: void/int declaration changes move register allocation (C0547); prototyping a `()` declaration changes promotion of narrow or float arguments and can reprototype a sibling (C0326, C0364); each such case falls back to a ledgered exception with verified cites.
- Parser coverage: argcheck sees one-line declarations only (DECL :48) and its comment masking is unverified; T4 checks the join's coverage against T1's raw counts before any fix-up relies on it.
- I5's names predate 3.43's renames: the list is mapped through config/names.tsv history (T1).
- tools-health time: the census adds to a 19-minute run; T3 records the cost, T9 holds the bound.
- Constraint R74: instruction text in a tracked file; the census stays in build/, cites stay short, audit_public runs at T10.
- The restruct ledger (541 MB, gitignored) gains KEPT rows if the new macro is ledgered there; a lost ledger turns the type gate red; ledger_backup runs at T10.
- dedup RETURN-LIE rows whose lie 3.44 clears keep a stale reason until 3.45 shares them.
- Ghidra: the running MCP blocks the proofs and its stop needs the developer's word; `make clean` wipes build/ghidra_rebuild/proj, so R22 and the proofs never overlap.
- Time: each batch costs a scratch compile and R22 (about 3 to 5 min); tools-health about 19 min at each task's end; T4's review is a stop.
- Disk: 24 GB free; the census and the per-object baselines go in build/ and .run/3.44/.

**🟪 Planning · Proposed rule T3**

> a lever removed by a readability edit drops its config/lever_residue.tsv row in the same commit.

In phase 3.43, giving one function a real return value removed a fake line that was there only to make the compiled bytes match. The project's list of those fake lines still had an entry for it, so the next full health check (about 19 minutes) failed on that stale entry until it was deleted and the check run again. This rule says the entry goes in the same commit as the code change, so no saved state ever fails the check. It costs nothing to build, and it matters again in 3.44, whose return-value edits may remove more of these fake lines.

**The retrospective: yes.** `docs/retrospective.md` has a Phase 43 clause in each of its four parts: what we believed, what failed, what it cost, and what to do sooner. The "sooner" part is your hindsight list:
- make the rename tool work one binary at a time before the first rename;
- put a time limit on every scan from the start;
- count how many names have outside evidence before planning a naming phase, so the plan expects guesses;
- treat a coder's work cut off by a restart as a draft.

The story has a Phase 43 part too.

**The day-1 guide: no, and that's the real gap.** The guide is `docs/how-to-ai-decomp/`, the chapters a new decomp would start from. Nothing in it mentions naming: no ledger, no `guess_` rule, no citation rule. 3.41 had a task that wrote its return-type lesson into the guide; 3.43's plan had no such task. So a new project started from our kit today would get the tools, which are up to date, but not the advice to name from day 1 with evidence. That advice would be:
- keep a names ledger from the first match;
- name only with a recorded source, and mark everything else as a best guess with its basis;
- make placeholder names specific to each binary.

**A README chart: I'd add one.** The readability series and its README graph track types, casts, levers and return lies, but nothing about names. A column set would show the post-100% work moving the way the timeline shows matching:
- named functions and data that are cited;
- names that are best guesses;
- placeholders still left, like `func_80…` and `D_80…`.

The day-1 guide (`docs/how-to-ai-decomp/`, especially chapter 01 on governance) and the kit describe the workflow as it was when they were written. Nobody has checked them against how PA3 actually runs: approved plans run on their own, there are experts, coders and retrievers, records filed from conversation, rules and the cookbook, and the planner drafts plans. So it's a methodology audit, not a find-and-replace. That's why it deserves its own phase.

**What the phase would do, as I'd brief its planner:**
- **Map PA3.** Write down how PA3 works today, from its own skill and docs and this project's history since the migration (3.38 to 3.44): what changed from PA2, and what this project learned using it.
- **Audit the kit against that map.** Check the day-1 guide, the wiki's "Start a new decomp project" and "How to AI decomp" pages, the kit manifest and corpora, and the README's "How the AI was used" section. Each stale passage gets one of three verdicts: rewrite, retire, or still true.
- **Rewrite** so a new decomp started from the kit follows PA3 from day 1. That includes the naming and signature lessons from 3.43 and 3.44.
- **Milestone:** the audit table shows 0 stale passages left, the links check is clean, and the kit corpus is regenerated. It changes no game code, so the bytes are untouched.

**Where it goes is your call.** My recommendation is right after 3.44, before layout. The new rule T5 has every phase write its lessons into the day-1 guide, so aligning the guide with PA3 early means layout's and validation's lessons land in the right shape. Generation validation should check the finished kit, not one still being rewritten. The cost is one more renumber: layout would become 3.46 and validation 3.47.

done

The struct map's counts now come out the same on every run of an unchanged tree. The verdicts are unchanged from T1, and the second `make tools-health` run is OK.

**Cause.** The bug was in `walk_all` in tools/type_census.py (pre-fix :1066-1079, now :1073-1086). Files that missed the walk cache were put into `results` first. Files that hit the cache were then assigned with `results[rel] = r`, which keeps each key's existing position. So `results.values()` listed the misses before the hits, and which files missed depended on which mtimes had changed. `build_struct_map` (:798-860) feeds its union-find from that order. The union-find refuses some merges (a width conflict, or no shared offset) depending on what was merged earlier, so a different order gives different clusters. A second, smaller difference: fresh walks were plain Python objects while cached ones had been through JSON.

**Fix.** Commit 23125e7899. I used a fixed order rather than a content-keyed cache, so the output no longer depends on cache state at all.
- `walk_all` now builds `results` in the sorted `files` order.
- A new `_walk_worker_json` puts fresh walks through the same JSON round trip as cached ones. `_walk_worker` itself is unchanged, because restruct.py calls it directly.
- The docs/struct-map.md stamp now carries only the commit, not the wall-clock time. With the time in it, no two runs could ever write a byte-identical doc (C0562).

**Proof.**

| Run | `struct_map:` (types / conflicts) | doc sha |
|---|---|---|
| Old code, partial cache (68 .c files touched), -j 16 | 14239 / 769 | ab40f289 |
| New code, cold cache, -j 16 | 14376 / 770 | c75f4f3e |
| New code, warm cache, -j 16 | 14376 / 770 | c75f4f3e |
| New code, partial cache (69 more touched), -j 8 | 14376 / 770 | c75f4f3e |

The type_census run inside tools-health printed the same line and left the doc's sha unchanged.

**Gates.**
- `--check`, `--check-structs` and `--check-casts --residue` equal T1's: 19 lying callees, 9,302 rows all ledgered, 0 uncovered sites, 0 unbacked macros. selftest is 73/73.
- The first tools-health run failed only on the stale kit corpus copy of type_census.py (tool_census GAP). `make kit-corpus` refreshed it and the rerun is OK.

**Commits.** The regenerated doc, cookbook C0582 and the corpus copy were committed once, in 7144af7183. Nothing was pushed.

**Deviations.** The plan named an in-house coder. The change was three edits plus verification, so I made it myself. I also removed the timestamp from the doc stamp, which the byte-identical check required.

**Follow-up.** tools/lever_census.py:864-875 has the same cache-fill pattern, and 3.43 T12 saw its printouts vary from run to run. It is out of this task's scope; C0582 describes the fix. I recommend a small task to apply it there.

No, the game doesn't have 14,000 structs. Your instinct is right that the real number is far smaller. My guess is a few hundred rather than 50, because a 1998 game this size would have had structs for actors, the camera, matrices, sprites, menus, save data, each boss's state and so on. I haven't measured that.

**What the 14,376 counts.** It isn't struct definitions, and it isn't instances either. It's the census tool's count of "access shapes" (`docs/struct-map.md`, line 5). The tool finds every place the code reads memory through a cast pointer, 172,948 places in all. It groups two of those places together only when there's hard evidence they're the same thing: the same global, or a pointer handed from one function to another. It never groups them just because the field offsets look alike. That rule keeps it from merging things wrongly, but it splits a lot. When two parts of the code touch the same real struct with no visible link between them, it counts two types. When a function reads only one field, it records a fragment; many entries have one field and are 2 bytes long.

**What's actually defined in the headers.** About 3,400 struct definitions, and about 3,100 of those still have placeholder names (`Unkstruct_…`). That's also too many, for the same reason: many are partial views of the same real struct.

**Why it hasn't been merged.** Merging two of these safely needs evidence that they're the same struct. Merging on looks alone risks giving a modder a wrong type. 3.43 also deliberately left struct types and field names for later. That was decision R110, made because the rename tool can't rename types or fields yet. Nothing in the current generation plan merges them.

**My recommendation:** note it in the inbox as a candidate phase for Generation 4. That phase would merge the fragments into the game's real types on evidence, then name the types and their fields, with each one's basis recorded in the names ledger. It doesn't belong in 3.44, which is about signatures. The picker is open.

The card line from the last filing's to-do was already rewritten to point at rule T5, so nothing was left to retire. I've released the talk hold, so T3 carries on.

**Why there:**
- **After signatures (3.44, running now).** Merging two struct fragments can change the type of a function's argument. Once 3.44 is done, its signature check catches any merge that breaks a function's real contract. Before that, nothing would.
- **Before file layout.** Layout groups the code into files and folders by game system. Real named types, such as an actor struct or a camera struct, show which system each header and file belongs to. Layout run on fragments would name files from `Unkstruct_` placeholders and then need redoing.
- **Before the kit rewrite.** That way the day-1 guide gets the struct lesson along with the naming and signature lessons.

**What 3.45 must deliver:**
- **Measure first.** Count the about 3,400 struct definitions in the headers, about 3,100 of them still placeholders, against the census's 14,376 fragments. The real target number comes out of that count.
- **Settle every placeholder struct.** Each one is either merged into its real type, kept apart with a written reason, or left with a recorded "no evidence" note. A tool checks that none is left unsettled.
  - A merge needs evidence: a shared global, a pointer passed between functions, shared code, or matching field widths in the machine code. A similar-looking layout is never enough.
- **Name the result.** The surviving types get names, and so do the fields of the most-used ones. Each name is cited or marked `guess_` with its basis, as in 3.43.
- **Tools.** The rename tool first learns to rename types and fields. It can't today, which is why 3.43 left structs out.
- **The usual gates.** All 218 binaries still rebuild byte-identical, the type check passes, and the types in Ghidra are rewritten to match and pass the six proofs. No files move.

**Housekeeping that came with the renumber:**
- Two deferred inbox items now point at their new phases: your folder-layout goal at 3.46, and the license at 3.48.
- The plan's ordering notes explain where 3.45 sits.

3.44 itself is unchanged, and T3 carries on.

Tail uses settle by a fixed point in strongly-connected-component order, and cycles come out as `recursion`.
- Selftest: 29 checks PASS; I re-ran it myself.
- `-j 16` takes 17.9 s and 17.0 s, and the two runs are cmp-identical.
- `make kit-corpus` is clean, `make tools-health` is OK, and the registry rows are in.
- docs/ops/sig-evidence.md states every rule and reason with its source.
- Commits: ef8da51d64, 16f4a4934c, 231f3e07af, a05df97612.

Results over 92,645 classes:

| Verdict | Classes |
|---|---|
| used | 11,324 |
| unused | 18,020 |
| unknown | 63,301 |

The unknowns split by verdict reason as: indirect call 39,456, no callers 8,815, tail position unresolved 7,094, address taken 6,286, cross-binary target unresolved 1,644, path leaves body 5, recursion 1, jump table with $v0 live 0.

Hand checks against objdump found one real bug: calls from modules into overlays were dropped, because a module's splat stack leaves out its overlay. It is fixed by resolving targets outside the stack by function start fleet-wide (C0585).

The other controls hold:
- Every name 3.41 flipped is `used` or carries a reason.
- All 20 random rows are OK.
- An independent cross-check of `no callers` and `indirect call` rows came back 30 of 30 clean.

The question is control (4) part one. The census agrees with objdump on all 19 lying_exceptions callees, but the shape the plan expects (the callee narrows before `jr $ra` and some caller reads $v0 unextended) holds for only 11. The bytes refute it for the other 8:
- func_8002A27C/4C8/738/9A8 exit through `lw v0`.
- func_800167F0 exits `xori v0,1`, and all 506 of its reads are `andi 0xffff`.
- func_801633A8 exits with no narrowing.
- func_80188F10's only reads are `sll 16`.
- guess_RequestSound has 0 reads across 7,026 sites, so it is `tail position unresolved`.

For these 8 the ledger's cause is a conversion on the caller's side. I did not redefine the check.

A second finding: 146 linked functions have no sig row, 73 in main and 73 in resident (for example func_80014554 and the four func_8002A27C family callees). They therefore have no census row.

Recommendation: accept control (4) part one as measured and mark T3 done. Give the 146-function sig gap to T4 as its first step, either by fixing the sig-main and sig-resident seeds or by having `--compare` report those functions as uncovered.

Checking it by hand against the disassembler turned up one real bug. Calls from always-loaded code into overlays (code loaded per area) were being missed, and that made some functions look unused when they aren't. It's fixed.
